visible_copy.title: Shared login: a proposal to examine
body: Expected benefit: less repeated access work

visual_plan.subject: one personal identity across services

visual_plan.approximate_composition: account at left; three services stacked at right; restrained connecting lines

speaker_notes.text:
Hi everyone.

I want to walk through a shared login proposal and the trade-offs it brings.

The idea we will examine is one personal account across services. We expect that could reduce some repeated access work, but we do not have measurements yet.

Let me start with the access pattern we are using as a working assumption.
speaker_notes.transition: Move from the proposal to the current-pattern assumption

slides.purpose: Understand the illustrative current pattern and the need to confirm it

audience_state.before: Know this is an unmeasured proposal
audience_state.after: Understand the illustrative current pattern and the need to confirm it

visual_plan.subject: assumed current access pattern
relationships: each illustrative service has a separate account path
visual_plan.approximate_composition: three separate horizontal paths; no shared identity hub

source_mapping.visible_copy: proposed working assumption, not supplied organization fact
source_mapping.speaker_notes: proposed working assumption, not supplied organization fact

speaker_notes.text:
Imagine a colleague moving between three services. This is an illustration, not a report about a particular person.

For the discussion, I am assuming each service has its own account and access steps. That can mean choosing credentials again or dealing with recovery separately.

We need to confirm that pattern against our actual environment. With that assumption visible, we can look at what the proposal changes.
speaker_notes.transition: Compare the separate paths with the proposed shared identity

slides.purpose: Distinguish personal identity, conditional session reuse and service permissions

audience_state.after: Distinguish personal identity, conditional session reuse and service permissions

visual_plan.subject: proposed identity/session model with separate permissions
objects: a gate inside each service boundary
relationships: session reuse is conditional on service support
permissions are checked at each service
visual_plan.approximate_composition: shared identity hub across top; three service boundaries below, each with its own small gate

speaker_notes.text:
Now, here is the model I propose we discuss. The account belongs to one person and can be recognised across services.

Where a service supports it, the sign-in session could be reused. That is a design condition to check, not something we have already proved.

Signing in tells a service who the person is. Permissions still decide what that person can do in that service. Keeping those responsibilities clear gives us a basis for discussing the benefit.
speaker_notes.transition: Explain the possible benefit mechanism without numerical claims

slides.purpose: Understand qualitative expected benefit without interpreting it as measured outcome

audience_state.before: Understand the proposed model and its conditions
audience_state.after: Understand qualitative expected benefit without interpreting it as measured outcome

visual_plan.subject: possible reduction in repeated access steps
relationships: current-pattern lane repeats separate account steps
proposed lane reuses the personal account; session reuse remains conditional
visual_plan.approximate_composition: two horizontal lanes; illustrate account/sign-in actions with icons; no times, percentages, bar lengths or invented metric

speaker_notes.text:
So, where might the time saving come from?

First, a person could have fewer account credentials to keep track of. Second, where session reuse works, they may avoid some repeated sign-in steps as they move between services.

Those are the mechanisms we expect to help. We cannot say how much time they save yet, and the benefit will depend on how people actually move between services.

Now let us look at the questions that come with sharing the sign-in path.
speaker_notes.transition: Move from possible benefit to trade-offs

slides.purpose: Recognise common dependency, account lifecycle and permissions as unresolved trade-offs

audience_state.before: Know the expected benefit is unmeasured
audience_state.after: Recognise common dependency, account lifecycle and permissions as unresolved trade-offs

visual_plan.subject: questions raised by a shared identity path
relationships: services depend on a shared identity path
account lifecycle affects the shared identity
provider permissions still have distinct owners
visual_plan.approximate_composition: three equally weighted panels; show dependency, recovery and permission concepts; no severity ranking

speaker_notes.text:
A shared sign-in path gives us a common dependency to design carefully. What should happen if that path is unavailable?

We also need a clear account lifecycle. Who helps with recovery, and how should access be removed when it is no longer appropriate?

Then there is ownership: who manages the personal account, and who grants access inside each provider? These are investigation questions. I am not presenting settled implementation decisions.

That leaves us with a useful set of questions for the engineering discussion.
speaker_notes.transition: Turn unresolved trade-offs into discussion questions

audience_state.after: Be ready to discuss evidence and design questions without an implied rollout commitment

visible_copy.title: Questions for investigation
body: Which trade-offs need a design spike?
How would we evaluate a trial?

visual_plan.subject: questions that connect the proposal to possible investigation
relationships: trade-offs inform a possible design spike
a trial would need agreed evaluation criteria
visual_plan.approximate_composition: inputs on the left; three question cards on the right; an open discussion area, no assigned people or dates

speaker_notes.text:
So, we have a proposal, a possible benefit mechanism and a set of trade-offs.

I would like us to check which assumptions need evidence and which design questions deserve a small investigation. If we later choose a trial, we should agree how to evaluate it before claiming a saving.

What have we missed, and where would you start?
